newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Socialists win two-thirds in key vote.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Socialists win two-thirds in key vote.

text.p: Albania's ex-communist Socialists and their allies have won a two thirds majority in crucial polls called to end months of anarchy, election officials said on Wednesday, enabling them to push through vital legislation.

The central election commission said that following two rounds of voting on June 29 and July 6, the Socialist group had won at least 107 of the 155 parliamentary seats, above the 103 needed for a two-thirds majority.
With a handful of results still to be decided, figures showed the Socialists and their allies had 87 of the 115 seats decided by a straight majority vote.
The Socialists alone won more than 50 percent of 40 seats decided on a proportional basis, giving them at least 20 more seats.
The right-wing Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha lagged badly back with around 30 seats.
The Democrats, in power since 1992, won a landslide in elections last May which were boycotted by the opposition and branded as seriously flawed by international monitors.
But the collapse of shady pyramid schemes earlier this year, bankrupting thousands of families, sparked a violent uprising against the government for allowing the scams to flourish.

International monitors said the election was less than perfect, particularly in the south which is not under government control and where the Democrats could not effectively campaign, but described the process as adequate in the circumstances.

The sweeping majority will ensure that the new parliament can appoint a new head of state to replace Berisha should he fail to honour a promise to step down once the leftist government headed by Socialist leader Fatos Nano is installed.

However, Berisha, originally backed by the West for introducing market reforms but since criticised for his increasingly authoritarian rule, has indicated he is ready to step down and has already moved belongings from the presidential office.
Diplomats said on Wednesday they understood the new parliament could be convened within 48 hours and a new government sworn in by the end of next week.
This would be earlier than Nano had suggested, saying in interviews this week he expected parliament to be in place by July 20 and the government by July 25.

Berisha is expected to take over the leadership of the Democratic Party, replacing party chairman Tritan Shehu who resigned on Monday after winning only 29 percent of the vote in Kavaje near Tirana in Sunday's runoff.

The new president is expected to be Socialist Secretary-General Rexhep Mejdani, a 52-year-old physics professor. Nano has indicated he wants to reduce the head of state's powers, which grew dramatically under Berisha.

Nano, who was jailed by Berisha on corruption charges the Socialists said were politically motivated, has insisted his reformed party has nothing in common with the Stalinist regime of Enver Hoxha that ruled for 45 years.
Diplomats expect his government to continue market reforms, cooperate with international financial institutions and reform state institutions which crumbled earlier this year.

His first task will be to restore law and order, rebuilding the police and armed forces which disintegrated last March after civilians looted an estimated one million weapons from army barracks, speaking an orgy of violence in which at least 1,500 people died.
